title: Not the jug (Avot 4:20)
hookLine: look not at the flask, but at what is inside it

lines: TWO SAGES, AND JUGS OF WINE.
cards: At a wine shop, there's a bottle with a gorgeous label, heavy glass, a wax seal. Next to it, a plain bottle with a label that looks like it was printed at home. The hand drifts toward the fancy one.

Sometimes what's inside is thin and sour, and the plain bottle would've been wonderful. People get sorted the same way. The young intern, the older colleague, the guy with the accent, the woman in the wrong clothes.
Near the end of chapter four, two sages argue about exactly this, using jugs of wine.

teach.b: One sage says: learning from the young is like eating unripe grapes and drinking wine straight from the press. Learning from the old is like eating ripe grapes and drinking aged wine. Experience matters, he's saying.
Go to the elders. Then Rabbi Meir answers him. Don't look at the jug.

teach.h: A NEW JUG FULL OF OLD WINE.
teach.b: There's a new jug full of old wine, and an old jug that doesn't even have new wine in it. A young person can hold deep, mature wisdom, and an old person can be empty. The container tells you nothing for sure.
You have to taste. The Bible says something close to this when the prophet Samuel, choosing a king, is impressed by Jesse's tall eldest son, Eliab.

In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, God tells him, "for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." The chosen one turns out to be the youngest, out with the sheep.
Rabbi Meir lived this. His own teacher, Elisha ben Abuyah, later left the path of the sages, and the others called him simply acher, the other one.
The Talmud asks how Rabbi Meir could keep learning from him, and answers with a picture: he found a pomegranate, ate what was inside, and threw away the peel.
That doesn't mean age and experience don't matter. It means you don't get to skip the tasting. Every person has to be met for what they actually hold.

how: Rabbi Meir's saying is often quoted in Jewish teaching as a reminder not to judge people or ideas by appearance, age or background.

o: the sage who said: learn from the old, like aged wine
the sage who said: don't look at the jug, but what's in it
the sage who said: judge the wine by its seal

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.
p: eat the inside, throw the peel

s: Rabbi Meir says only the old are worth learning from
he answers that very idea: a new jug can hold old wine.
Rabbi Meir kept learning from a teacher who left the path
he ate the pomegranate and threw away the peel.
Rabbi Meir says age and experience never matter
he says you can't judge by the container. you have to taste.

games.q: you're Rabbi Meir. your great teacher has left the path, and everyone says stop learning from him. what do you do?
o: stop. a teacher like that has nothing to give.
keep learning: eat the fruit, throw away the peel.
keep learning everything, peel and all.
games.why: the Talmud says he found a pomegranate, ate what was inside, and threw away the peel.

practice: Think of someone you've quietly sorted by their outside: too young to know anything, too old to get it, too loud, too plain, too different.
Picture their face, set the label down, and wonder what's actually inside them, what they've lived through, what they might know. Stay curious for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Rabbi Meir, whose rule was: don't look at the container, look at what's in it. A new jug can hold old wine, and an old jug may hold none at all.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: don't look at the jug.

carryVoice: Your line: you have to taste. A plain jug can hold old wine. See you tomorrow.
